newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers gloomy on upcoming talks.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers gloomy on upcoming talks.

text.p: Employers in Germany's metal and engineering industries only see a slight chance of agreeing on cuts in labour costs with unions this month after two earlier rounds failed, their chief negotiator said on Wednesday.
Asked about forthcoming talks in North Rhine-Westphalia, Werner Stumpfe of the Gesamtmetaall employers federation said "I don't look forward to them with great optimism."

Previous talks on how to implement new 20-percent cuts in sick pay failed at a national level and subsequently, in the southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemburg. Discussions are likely to drag into the 1997 pay round in January, he said.
Stumpfe told journalists the Baden-Wuerttemburg talks had come very close to a compromise but failed after the IG Metall trade union overruled its regional negotiators.
The sticking point was scrapping entitlement to days off accrued when workers are absent due to illness, he said.
"We received a green light for four weeks, and the other side pulled out of its offer of three weeks," Stumpfe said.

The attempt to impose sick pay cuts has triggered a bitter row that has led to major union demonstrations and walkouts across Germany. Union leaders fear benefits accumulated since World War Two will be eroded if sick pay entitlements are cut.
But German employers say they are handicapped by high wage costs, social security overheads, short working hours and long holidays -- all of which are forcing people out of work.
German unemployment hit a post-unification high in October of four million, and the metal and engineering industries are haemorrhaging 140,000 jobs a year.
Stumpfe said it was vital to push through the sick pay cuts to demonstrate Germany's ability to reform its economic system and act as a signal to encourage foreign investment.
But, he said, trade unions were under pressure from their members to protect labour perks and oppose reforms.
